name: Beth Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day, and what you did for work before, if you did.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at six, same as when I worked, and put the kettle on. I walk down to Hartley Green's high street to look in the shop windows for cards saying 'help wanted', and I ring the numbers from the newsagent's board. Wednesdays I help at the church hall lunch, and Sunday I sing in the choir. For eleven years I worked at Petal and Stem, the florist on the corner, until the owner, Mrs Okafor, closed in June. Supermarket bouquets and the phone-ordering firms did for her, not for lack of trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that sounds sensible to me. Fuss and fashion come and go, and people still need food, flowers and a kind word. I'd be glad if things went on as they were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of noise about machines, and the real trouble is that small shops can't compete with the big firms. I'd tell the ladies at church that a computer can't arrange a wedding bouquet to a bride's mother's liking. I'd say it quietly, mind, I don't like to make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I don't fear the AI so much as the big companies who let the high street die. Mrs Okafor did everything right, early mornings, fair prices, loyal customers, and still closed. I'd say what's left for me is a shop job, and they're being cut one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep walking the high street and ringing numbers, and I'd call in at every florist, garden centre and bakery within a bus ride. I'd ask the vicar and the church ladies if they know of anyone hiring, because word of mouth has always worked for me. I'd stay clear of those job websites, because I can't make head or tail of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but low. I'm not frightened, but I'm lonely some days, and ashamed to be on benefits, which I've never been before. Work gave me a reason to get up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the shame feel like in a normal week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the queue at the jobcentre, and the lady behind the glass who calls me by my surname. I feel I should have kept the shop going somehow, which is silly. I'd far rather earn my own money than be given it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask first about a job, and what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Brennan at the garden centre, who knew me from the flower shop. I'd say I'm reliable, I know my plants, and I'll work Saturdays. I'd not ask for much money, just a fair wage and a chance.

say: I'd say it's a lot of noise, and the real trouble is **small shops** can't compete with big firms.
I'd say a computer can't arrange a **wedding bouquet** to a bride's mother's liking.
think: I fear the **big companies** that let the high street die more than AI.
Mrs Okafor did everything right and still **closed**.
do: Walk the **high street** and ring numbers from the newsagent's board.
Call in at every florist, garden centre and bakery within a **bus ride**.
Ask the **vicar** and church ladies who is hiring.
feel: Steady but low, **ashamed** to be on benefits for the first time.
S0.quote: I'd far rather earn my own money than be given it.
fieldNote: Her pain is **shame**, not fear of technology.
Blames **big firms** and supermarkets for the closed shop, and cites her old boss as proof it wasn't poor effort.
Relies on **word of mouth** and church ties, avoids job websites.

steps.text: Call in at every florist, garden centre and bakery within a bus ride
Ask the vicar and the church ladies who is hiring
Keep walking the high street for help wanted cards each morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second one. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a bigger thing. Writing, booking, answering customers, those are what the girls at the supermarket head office did, I suppose. I'd say my own job with the flowers would be safe for a good while, but I wouldn't like to be certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines may take the paperwork, but people still need people, and we should look after those who lose out. I'd say employers should train their staff before they replace them, as a matter of decency. I'd also say apprenticeships are better than handouts, and I'd say it to the church group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think shops will want fewer people, and the ones left will have to run tills and order stock on a screen. That's the bit I find hard, and I've never been quick with computers. I'd worry that at my age I'd be passed over for someone who can do the screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for work that's mostly with hands and people: garden centre, bakery, care home kitchen. I'd ask the church for help finding a place where someone could show me the computers slowly, in person. I'd take whatever small job I could while I wait, like cleaning at the church hall for a few pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a plain way, like a tight belt. I'd be praying more, I'd say, and trying not to be grumpy with my neighbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'someone to show me slowly' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person beside me at a table, not a video. Our neighbour's boy, Daniel, showed me how to send a text last year in about ten minutes. I'd say with a good teacher I could learn, but I won't be pushed, and I won't pretend I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said apprenticeships beat handouts. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because an apprenticeship gives you a trade and your pride. A handout gives you a number on a form. I've nothing against help when you need it, but I'd rather the help led to a job.

say: I'd say machines may take the paperwork, but **people need people**.
I'd say apprenticeships are **better than handouts**.
think: Shops will want fewer people, and the rest must run **tills and stock** on a screen.
At my age I'd be **passed over** for someone good with screens.
do: Go for **hands-on work**: garden centre, bakery or a care home kitchen.
Ask the church for help finding someone to teach me **computers slowly**.
Take small jobs like cleaning the **church hall** while I wait.
feel: Anxious in a plain way, like a **tight belt**.
S1.quote: An apprenticeship gives you a trade and your pride. A handout gives you a number on a form.
fieldNote: Her **outlook** shows: work and apprenticeships over handouts.
Will learn computers only from **a person beside her**, not a video.
Hands-on jobs seem safer to her, but she fears being passed over.

steps.text: Apply for work at the garden centre, bakery and care home kitchen
Ask Daniel next door to teach me the computer in person
Enrol in an in-person computer basics class at the library

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's no time at all. I'd say that's frightening, and I'd have to sit down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it needs the government and the churches and the families all pulling together, and quickly. I'd say we can't leave people to fall through the cracks. I'd also say we must keep faith that people have value beyond what a machine can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be frightened out of my wits. If the thinking jobs go in two years, the shops and offices go with them, and everyone will be hunting for what's left, which is hands-on work. I'm thirty-four with no savings and no great qualifications, and I'd be at the back of the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the church and the food bank early, before the rush, and tell them what's coming. I'd cut every penny: no more sweets, no more bus, I'd walk everywhere. I'd also hold on to my little flat by asking the landlord, Mr Patel, to agree a payment plan, since he's a decent man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened and sick, and I'd be praying in the night. I'd feel sorry for everyone, not just me. It would feel like standing in a field when the storm is coming and nowhere to shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the church group that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we must open the hall on weekdays for people to come and talk and eat together. I'd say we must look after each other, because the government will be slow. That's what a church is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it help that robots are about three years behind the thinking machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, because hands-on work lasts longer. But I'd fear the queues for the few jobs, and the wages falling. A florist is a hands job, but who buys flowers when no one has work?

say: I'd say it needs **government, churches and families** pulling together quickly.
I'd say we must keep faith that people have **value** beyond what a machine can do.
think: If thinking jobs go in two years, everyone hunts for **hands-on work**.
I'm thirty-four with **no savings** and would be at the back of the queue.
do: Go to the church and **food bank** early and tell them what's coming.
Cut every penny and **walk everywhere** instead of taking the bus.
Ask my landlord Mr Patel for a **payment plan**.
feel: Frightened and sick, like standing in a field with a **storm** coming.
S2.quote: A florist is a hands job, but who buys flowers when no one has work?
fieldNote: Looks to the **church community** as her safety net.
Sees the demand problem: **no wages** means no flowers.
Her fear grows because she expects to be at the back of a long queue.

steps.text: Visit the church food bank and the vicar in the first week
Walk everywhere and stop buying sweets and bus tickets
Open the church hall on weekdays for a shared lunch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is something I could just about get my head around. It's still very fast, but there's a little room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do right by people, if we start right now: apprenticeships, fair pay, and families supported to look after their own. I'd say the churches and councils should work together. I'd be sorry to see people left on benefits with no purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I could get into a hands-on job in the next year, a garden centre or a care kitchen, and hold on for the five years. After that I don't know. I'd be thirty-nine, and I'd hope I'd have saved enough to do something small of my own, like a market stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for an apprenticeship or a steady job at a garden centre, and learn what I can there. I'd put a little by every pay day in a post office account. I'd start a small stall selling dried flowers and wreaths at the church fair, to learn about running something myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhat easier. It's like a long hill, and at least I can see the path up it. I'd still feel anxious about the first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the market stall mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be my own little corner, where I'd be answerable to nobody but the customers. Mrs Okafor, my old boss, started with a stall, and she told me that's how you learn what people really want. If she could do that, so could I, and I think she'd be glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in the middle of that five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the garden centre job doesn't come, and my benefits get cut for not trying hard enough. That happened to a woman at church. I'd worry about being stuck between the rules and the jobs, with nobody to speak for me.

say: I'd say five years is enough to do right by people with **apprenticeships** and fair pay.
I'd say churches and councils should **work together**.
think: I could get a **hands-on job** next year and hold on for five years.
At thirty-nine I'd hope to start a small **market stall**.
do: Look for an **apprenticeship** or steady job at a garden centre.
Put a little in a **post office** account every pay day.
Start a small stall of **dried flowers** at the church fair.
feel: Somewhat easier, like a long hill where I can see the **path** up.
S3.quote: Mrs Okafor, my old boss, started with a stall, and she told me that's how you learn what people really want.
fieldNote: Draws on her **old boss's example** to imagine a stall.
Fears a benefits **sanction** more than any technology.
The extra time lets her plan one small, realistic step.

steps.text: Apply for an apprenticeship or steady job at the garden centre
Put a little in a post office account every pay day
Run a dried flower and wreath stall at the church fair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, now. That feels almost kind. I'll be forty-four, still able-bodied, and with time to learn something new if it comes to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair length of time to put things right: apprenticeships, family support, real jobs, and keeping communities together. I'd say don't wait until the last minute. We have a chance to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be all right, I really do. I'd find a hands-on job, keep my church and my choir, save a little each month, maybe even run a small flower stall properly. The worry underneath is whether the big firms will take all the benefit and leave the high street to wither.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a steady job in the first year, then save for a lease on a little shop unit, or at least a regular market pitch. I'd take an evening course on shop books and ordering, in person, once I'm earning. I'd also ask Daniel next door to show me the computer a bit at a time, so I'm not a stranger to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with a quiet hope. Ten years is long enough to get back my confidence and rebuild.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good life look like for you in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small shop or stall with my name on it, a flat that's mine to keep clean, and the choir on Sundays. I'd have Wednesday lunches at the hall and someone younger I'm training up. That would be enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still knock that plan off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big firms squeeze the small ones even harder, or the rent on a shop unit goes through the roof. I'd also worry about my own health, because I've bad knees from standing all day. But I'd manage, with help from the church and good friends.

say: I'd say ten years is a fair time to put things right with **apprenticeships** and family support.
I'd say don't wait until the **last minute**.
think: I'd find a hands-on job, keep my **church and choir**, and save monthly.
I worry **big firms** will take the benefit and leave the high street to wither.
do: Get a steady job in year one and save for a **market pitch** or shop unit.
Take an in-person evening course on shop **books and ordering**.
Have Daniel next door show me the **computer** a bit at a time.
feel: Fairly calm with a **quiet hope**, enough to rebuild my confidence.
S4.quote: A small shop or stall with my name on it, a flat that's mine to keep clean, and the choir on Sundays.
fieldNote: Her ideal is **small and rooted**: stall, flat, choir, a trainee.
Bad knees and **rent costs** are named risks, which keeps her mood anxious.
Ten years softens her fear of computers into a slow plan.

steps.text: Take a steady garden centre job and learn the trade
Save toward a market pitch or a small shop unit
Take an in-person evening course on shop books and ordering
Train up a younger helper once the stall is running

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 frightens me most. Two years is no time for a woman with no savings and no skill with screens, and the shops would be the first to go quiet. What would help is jobs I can do with my hands, someone to teach me the computer in person, and the church and community looking after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not asking for charity. I'd far rather work than sit on benefits. If somebody could give a woman my age a chance and a fair wage, they'd get an honest day's work.

headlineQuote: I'm not asking for charity. I'd far rather work than sit on benefits.
portrait: Beth is **34**, lives alone in Hartley Green, and has had **benefits only** since her florist shop closed in June.
She worked eleven years at Petal and Stem, and her real pain is **shame** at being on benefits, not fear of machines.
She avoids computers and AI, leans on **church** and **word of mouth**, and wants work and apprenticeships over handouts.
She blames big firms and supermarkets, and is anxious in most scenarios, **alarmed** at two years.
She dreams of a small stall or shop with her **own name** on it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is no time with no savings and no skill with screens.
whatWouldHelp: **Hands-on jobs** and someone to teach her the computer in person.
A **community** that looks after its own through the church.
